provenance.basis: Bates 13e p. XXX [verify]; StatPearls NBK541010 (S1 loudest at apex, 50-150 Hz [verify])
Bates 13e p. XXX [verify]; StatPearls NBK541010 (S2 loudest at base, higher pitch than S1 [verify])

card.summary: Two crisp sounds per beat and nothing between them. S1 is loudest at the apex; S2 is loudest at the base. Systole is the short gap, diastole the long one.
card.why: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing as the ventricles start to contract, so it is loudest where the ventricles sit against the chest wall, at the apex. S2 is the aortic and pulmonic valves closing at the end of ejection, so it is loudest at the base where the great vessels come closest to the surface.
card.why_squared: At 72 bpm the cycle is about 830 ms. Systole is roughly fixed at about 300 ms [verify: 250-330 ms], so diastole is about 530 ms. When rate rises, only diastole shortens. That is why extra diastolic sounds crowd together in tachycardia. [cite Bates 13e p. XXX; StatPearls NBK541010]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. [page - verify]
Dornbush S, Turnquest AE. Physiology, Heart Sounds. StatPearls. NBK541010.

quiz_rationales.identify: Two sounds per beat, S1 then S2, with a short silent systole and a longer silent diastole. Nothing extra: this is normal.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_s3: Switch to the bell at the apex and listen just after S2. There is nothing there. No S3.
quiz_rationales.which_head: Either head. S1 and S2 sit in a band both heads pass. Neither reveals anything the other hides here.
quiz_rationales.timing: There is no murmur to time. Systole is the short gap after S1; diastole is the long gap after S2.
quiz_rationales.radiation: Nothing to follow. Both sounds fade evenly as you move off the precordium.

provenance.basis: Bates 13e p. XXX [verify] (aortic ejection murmur: mid-systolic, crescendo-decrescendo, harsh, radiates to carotids); Freeman & Levine 1933 (grading); CirCor DigiScope descriptor vocabulary

card.summary: A harsh murmur that starts after S1, swells to a peak in mid-systole and fades before S2. Loudest at the aortic area, it carries up into the neck and is faint at the apex.
card.why: Blood is being pushed through a narrowed outlet. Flow ramps up as the ventricle contracts, peaks, and falls off, so the noise follows the same crescendo-decrescendo shape. Turbulence is generated at the valve, at the base, and the jet points up the aorta toward the carotids, which is where the sound travels.
card.why_squared: The murmur stops before S2 because ejection ends before the valve closes; a murmur that runs through S2 is not an ejection murmur. Follow it up the neck and it stays; follow it to the axilla and it goes. That direction of radiation is the finding a chart note should carry. Grades IV and above come with a palpable thrill, which no recording can teach. [cite Bates 13e p. XXX; Freeman & Levine 1933]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. [page - verify]
Dornbush S, Turnquest AE. Physiology, Heart Sounds. StatPearls. NBK541010.
Freeman AR, Levine SA. The clinical significance of the systolic murmur. Ann Intern Med. 1933;6:1371-1385.
Oliveira J, et al. The CirCor DigiScope Phonocardiogram Dataset (v1.0.3). PhysioNet, 2022. doi:10.13026/tshs-mw03

quiz_rationales.identify: Between S1 and S2 there is a rough noise that grows and then fades. That is a systolic murmur with a crescendo-decrescendo shape.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_s3: Bell at the apex, listen after S2: nothing. There is no S3 here; the finding is in systole.
quiz_rationales.localize: It is loudest at the aortic area, right of the sternum in the second space. It stays strong up toward the right clavicle and neck and drops away toward the apex.
quiz_rationales.which_head: The diaphragm. The murmur is medium to high pitched and harsh; the bell muffles it.
quiz_rationales.timing: The murmur sits between S1 and S2 and stops before S2. Systolic.
quiz_rationales.radiation: Follow it up the neck: it is still there over the carotid. Toward the axilla it is gone. Carotids.

provenance.basis: Bates 13e, abdomen chapter [verify]: normal bowel sounds 5-34 per minute, gurgles and clicks, transmitted widely

sources.label: toward the chest: the heart, distant

card.summary: Soft, irregular gurgles and clicks every few seconds, varying in pitch, heard much the same anywhere on the abdomen. Between them, quiet.
card.why: Each gurgle is gas and fluid being pushed along by a wave of peristalsis. The gut moves in irregular bursts, so the sounds come in irregular bursts. They travel through the abdomen, so one listening spot hears the whole gut.
card.why_squared: Normal is about 5 to 34 sounds a minute [verify], with wide variation by time since a meal. Because sounds transmit across the abdomen, hearing them in one quadrant is enough to chart them as present; you do not need all four. [cite Bates 13e abdomen chapter, page to verify]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. Abdomen. [page - verify]

quiz_rationales.identify: Gurgles every few seconds, irregular, mixed pitch, no long silences. That is an active, normal bowel.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_active: Wait a few seconds and a gurgle comes. Bowel sounds are present and active.
quiz_rationales.which_head: The diaphragm. Bowel sounds are mid to high pitched clicks and gurgles; the bell dulls them.

provenance.basis: Bates 13e, abdomen chapter [verify]: hyperactive bowel sounds are frequent, loud, high-pitched; rushes and tinkles

sources.label: toward the chest: the heart, distant

card.summary: Frequent, loud sounds with barely a pause: high-pitched tinkles mixed with rushes of gurgling. The whole abdomen is busy.
card.why: The gut is contracting harder and more often than usual, pushing gas and fluid through with force. The higher pitch comes from gas squeezed through narrower, tighter loops of bowel.
card.why_squared: Chart what you hear: frequent, high-pitched, with rushes. Do not chart what it might mean; the same sounds appear in very different situations, and the rest of the assessment decides. Loud, high-pitched tinkles above 30 a minute [verify] is the pattern to name. [cite Bates 13e abdomen chapter, page to verify]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. Abdomen. [page - verify]

quiz_rationales.identify: Sounds almost continuously, many of them high and tinkling, with rushes. That is hyperactive, not merely active.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_active: Sounds are present, but far more frequent and higher pitched than normal. Present, yes; active in the normal sense, no: this is hyperactive.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_hyperactive: More than one sound every two seconds, high-pitched tinkles among them. Hyperactive.
quiz_rationales.which_head: The diaphragm. The tinkles are high pitched and the diaphragm brings them forward.

provenance.basis: Bates 13e, abdomen chapter [verify]: hypoactive bowel sounds are infrequent and soft

sources.label: toward the chest: the heart, distant

card.summary: Long quiet stretches with an occasional soft gurgle, perhaps one every twenty to thirty seconds. Mostly you hear the distant heart and breathing.
card.why: The gut is moving less than usual, so gas and fluid are pushed along less often. Fewer waves, fewer sounds, and softer ones.
card.why_squared: Fewer than about 5 sounds a minute is hypoactive [verify]. The trap is calling a quiet abdomen absent too soon: hypoactive still has sounds if you wait. Time the listening, do not guess it. [cite Bates 13e abdomen chapter, page to verify]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. Abdomen. [page - verify]

quiz_rationales.identify: Mostly silence, then one soft gurgle, then silence again. Sounds are there but few and faint: hypoactive.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_active: Sounds are present but infrequent and soft. Not active in the normal sense; this is hypoactive.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_hypoactive: Wait it out: one soft gurgle in twenty or thirty seconds. Hypoactive.
quiz_rationales.which_head: The diaphragm. The few sounds there are sit in its range.

provenance.basis: Bates 13e, abdomen chapter [verify]: absent means no sounds after listening for two minutes [verify: some sources teach five]

sources.label: toward the chest: the heart, distant

card.summary: Nothing from the gut. The distant heart and breathing are all you hear, however long you wait.
card.why: No peristalsis, no movement of gas and fluid, no sound. The abdomen is not silent, because the heart and lungs transmit through it, but the gut has stopped contributing.
card.why_squared: Absent is a finding you earn by waiting: listen for two full minutes [verify: some sources teach five] before writing it. The tool cannot make you wait, so treat thirty quiet seconds here as a prompt to keep listening, not as proof. [cite Bates 13e abdomen chapter, page to verify]
sources: Bickley LS. Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking, 13th ed. Abdomen. [page - verify]

quiz_rationales.identify: Listen through the whole clip: heart and breath only, no gurgle at all. Absent. At the bedside that verdict needs two full minutes.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_active: No gurgle, however long you wait. Bowel sounds are not present.
quiz_rationales.present_absent_bowel_absent: Not one sound from the gut. Absent, provided you have waited long enough to say so.
quiz_rationales.which_head: The diaphragm, which is the head you would use to be sure you are not missing a faint high-pitched sound.
